key_terms.meaning: A pin-jointed triangle-based framework of straight members loaded only at the joints, so every member carries axial force only
A member with forces applied at only two points and no weight or couple, so the two forces are equal, opposite and collinear
Solve a truss joint by joint using ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at each joint; 2 equations per joint, so start where only two unknowns meet
A member whose force is zero by inspection at a joint with two non-collinear members and no load, or three members with two collinear
Cut the truss through three unknown members, take one part as a free body and use ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 to get those three forces directly
A structure of interconnected members that is not a simple truss; members may be multi-force and carry bending, so it is split into separate free bodies
A frame designed to transmit or modify forces and do useful work, such as a toggle clamp or a nutcracker
The maximum friction a surface can supply just before sliding, F(max) = μN, where μ is the coefficient and N the normal reaction in newtons
The dimensionless ratio μ = F/N at impending motion; same value for static and kinetic only in the simplest textbook model
The angle between the resultant reaction and the normal, given by tan φ = μ, so φ = tan⁻¹ μ
The steepest angle of a rough plane at which a block just stays at rest; tan α = μ, so α equals the angle of friction

key_terms.term: Normal reaction on an incline N
key_terms.meaning: On a plane at angle θ to the horizontal, N = W cos θ newtons, with W the weight in newtons
On a rough incline the pushing force P lies between W sin θ − μW cos θ and W sin θ + μW cos θ, the two impending-sliding limits
A small-angle block pushed between two surfaces; friction on its two rough faces lets a small effort produce a large separating force
A ladder leaning on a wall and floor is a three-force-plus-friction rigid body; the floor friction f ≤ μN keeps the foot from slipping
For a flat belt on the point of slipping, T₂ = T₁ e^(μθ), where T₁ is the slack tension, T₂ the tight tension, θ the angle of contact in radians
The angle between the two sides of a V-belt groove; it replaces μ by μ/sin β, giving T₂ = T₁ e^(μθ/sin β)
Lead L is the axial distance the screw advances in one turn; tan α = L/(πd) with d the mean diameter and α the helix angle
A screw jack that stays up under load without the effort being held, which needs the friction angle φ ≥ helix angle α

key_terms.term: Mechanical advantage of a screw jack
key_terms.meaning: MA = W/P, the load divided by the effort; ideal MA = 2πr/L and efficiency η = tan α / tan(α + φ)

takeaways: A simple truss is solved because each joint gives only two equations, so you start where just two member forces are unknown and work outward.
The method of sections is faster when you need only a few member forces, because one cut and three equations give them without solving the whole truss.
Frames and machines must be dismembered, since a member with three or more forces is not a two-force member and its force direction is unknown.
Dry friction is bounded: the reaction can tilt up to the angle of friction φ = tan⁻¹ μ and no further, and that single idea solves most friction problems.
On a rough incline the friction limit shrinks with cos θ, so the safe range of the applied force narrows as the plane gets steeper.
A wedge, a screw jack and a belt all convert friction from a nuisance into a mechanism for multiplying force or gripping a load.
A V-belt grips far better than a flat belt of the same μ because the groove angle divides the effective coefficient by sin β.
A screw jack is efficient only when the helix angle is well above the friction angle, and those are exactly the conditions that stop it self-locking.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always pair a definition-and-derivation part (laws of friction, angle of repose, belt tension ratio, screw jack torque and efficiency) with a full numerical free-body solution, so keep the diagram, the assumed impending-motion direction and the units visible at every step.

bank.q: State the laws of dry friction and explain, with a neat sketch of the reaction cone, the terms limiting friction, coefficient of friction, angle of friction and angle of repose. Show that the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.
outline: Friction acts opposite to impending or actual relative motion, along the common tangent.
F(max) = μN; below this value friction equals the applied tangential force.
Reaction R tilts from the normal by φ where tan φ = μ; the cone of friction has semi-vertical angle φ.
On an incline at angle θ, equilibrium gives tan θ = μ at the point of slipping, so angle of repose = φ.
Static friction exceeds kinetic friction; note that μ is dimensionless and N is in newtons.

bank.q: Explain the assumptions of a simple truss and why each member becomes a two-force member. State the rule for identifying zero-force members with two examples.
outline: Members are straight, weightless, pin-jointed at ends, loads applied only at joints.
No bending moment or shear in a member, so force is axial: tension or compression.
Zero-force rule 1: two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint.
Zero-force rule 2: three members at an unloaded joint with two collinear.
A zero-force member may still carry force after the loading changes or for stability.

bank.q: Compare flat-belt and V-belt friction. Derive or state the tension ratio in each case and explain why the V-belt needs a smaller angle of contact.
outline: Flat belt: T₂ = T₁ e^(μθ), θ in radians.
V-belt: normal reaction is N/sin β for groove angle 2β, so μ becomes μ/sin β.
T₂ = T₁ e^(μθ/sin β); with β = 20° the factor is about 2.9 times the flat-belt value.
T₁ is slack side, T₂ tight side; ratio depends only on μ and θ.
Practical use: V-belts on a car engine or a flour mill transmit more torque without slipping.

bank.q: Define the terms used in a square-threaded screw: mean diameter, pitch, lead, helix angle, effort, mechanical advantage, efficiency and self-locking.
outline: Pitch = axial advance per thread; lead L = pitch × number of starts.
Helix angle tan α = L/(πd), d = mean diameter.
Unwinding the thread gives an inclined plane of angle α carrying the load W.
MA = W/P, ideal MA = 2πr/L with r the lever arm, efficiency η = tan α / tan(α + φ).
Self-locking when φ ≥ α, i.e. the load does not run the jack down by itself.

bank.q: A truss of a roof or a jib crane is loaded at its joints. Find all member forces by the method of joints and state whether each member is in tension or compression.
outline: Correct free-body diagram of the whole truss and support reactions from ΣM and ΣF.
Choose a joint with at most two unknowns; draw the joint free body with forces pulling away from the joint = tension.
Apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at each joint in sequence.
Tabulate member force magnitude, sign and tension/compression.
Check one joint not used earlier as a verification.

bank.q: For a given truss find the forces in three specified members using the method of sections, and verify one of them by the method of joints.
outline: Cut through not more than three unknown members, including the wanted ones.
Take the simpler part as the free body and show all external forces on it.
Use ΣM about a point where two cut members meet, to get the third directly.
Use ΣFy = 0 or ΣFx = 0 for a second member; resolve the third.
Sign convention and tension/compression statement; verify at a joint.

bank.q: A block of weight W rests on a rough plane inclined at θ to the horizontal. Find the range of a force applied parallel to the plane that keeps the block in equilibrium.
outline: Free body: W vertically down, N normal to plane, friction along plane, P parallel to plane.
Resolve along and normal to the plane: N = W cos θ.
Impending motion up: P = W sin θ + μW cos θ.
Impending motion down: P = W sin θ − μW cos θ.
So W(sin θ − μ cos θ) ≤ P ≤ W(sin θ + μ cos θ); if θ ≤ φ the block stays even with P = 0.

bank.q: A ladder of weight W and length L leans against a smooth vertical wall at angle θ to the ground. Find the minimum coefficient of friction at the floor for the ladder not to slip, and the reaction at the wall.
outline: Free body: W at mid-point, wall reaction R (horizontal, smooth wall), floor normal N and friction f.
ΣFx = 0 gives f = R; ΣFy = 0 gives N = W.
ΣM about the foot: R L sin θ = W (L/2) cos θ, so R = W cot θ / 2.
Limiting case f = μN gives μ = (cot θ)/2 as the minimum.
Comment: rougher floor or smaller θ; if the wall is also rough add a vertical friction term there.

bank.q: A screw jack with a square thread of mean diameter d and lead L raises a load W. Find the torque needed, the effort on a lever of length r, the efficiency and check self-locking.
outline: Unwrap the thread as an inclined plane at tan α = L/(πd).
Effort to raise: P = W tan(α + φ) at the mean radius, torque T = W (d/2) tan(α + φ).
Effort at the lever: P = T/r; MA = W/P = r/((d/2) tan(α + φ)).
Ideal torque = W L/(2π); efficiency η = tan α / tan(α + φ).
Self-locking if φ ≥ α, i.e. torque to lower would be negative.

bank.q: A wedge of angle 2α is driven between two blocks to lift a load W. Taking μ on all faces, find the effort needed to drive it in and to withdraw it.
outline: Free body of the wedge: effort P, reactions on both faces each tilted by φ from their normals.
Resolve vertically and horizontally, or use the triangle of forces.
Driving in: P = 2W tan(α + φ) for symmetric faces (state assumptions).
Withdrawing needs P = 2W tan(φ − α), which is negative if φ ≤ α, so the wedge self-locks.
State the role of friction angle and the practical case of a wedge for lifting a machine bed.

bank.q: A flat belt runs over a pulley with angle of contact θ and coefficient of friction μ, transmitting power at belt speed v. Find the maximum power transmitted and the tension ratio at slipping.
outline: T₂ = T₁ e^(μθ) at impending slip, θ in radians.
Power P = (T₂ − T₁) v watts with tensions in newtons and v in m/s.
For fixed maximum tension T₂, power peaks when T₁ = T₂/e^(μθ).
Centrifugal tension lowers the useful ratio at high speed.
Repeat for a V-belt with μ replaced by μ/sin β.

bank.q: A frame is loaded as shown and contains one member that is not a two-force member. Identify it, separate the frame into members, and find all pin reactions and the force in the two-force member.
outline: Test each member: forces at only two points and no load on it = two-force member.
Overall free body for external reactions at supports.
Dismember and draw each member's free body with internal pin forces equal and opposite.
Apply three equilibrium equations per multi-force member.
Check by taking moments about a pin for the whole frame; state magnitudes with units.

bank.q: For a given truss with inclined members and a load at an intermediate joint, identify all zero-force members, then find the forces in four specified members by the method of sections, and compare the effort with the method of joints.
outline: Apply the two zero-force rules systematically before any calculation.
Choose one or two cuts that pass through the wanted members.
Use ΣM about the intersection of two cut members to isolate the third.
Determine tension or compression from the assumed direction sign.
Evaluate: sections need fewer equations for a few members, joints are needed for all member forces.

bank.q: A ladder rests on a rough floor against a rough wall. Derive the condition for equilibrium, and evaluate whether the foot or the top will slip first as the inclination is decreased.
outline: Two friction limits: f_floor ≤ μ₁N_floor and f_wall ≤ μ₂N_wall, both unknown a priori.
Equations: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 give three equations with three unknowns plus two inequalities.
At limiting equilibrium at the foot, N_wall = μ₁N_floor and N_floor = W/(1 + μ₁μ₂).
Check whether the wall friction needed exceeds μ₂N_wall; if yes, the top slips first.
Conclude with the safe range of θ and the effect of a person standing part-way up.

bank.q: A screw jack is required both to raise a load easily and to hold it without a brake. Using the helix angle and friction angle, discuss the design trade-off, and compute the efficiency at the self-locking limit.
outline: Torque to raise T = W(d/2) tan(α + φ); efficiency η = tan α / tan(α + φ).
Larger α raises efficiency but reduces the margin of self-locking.
Self-locking needs φ ≥ α; at φ = α efficiency is tan α / tan 2α, that is, below 50 percent.
Friction angle depends on the thread and lubrication; square thread has lower φ than V-thread.
Recommendation: choose α well below φ for safety, accept low efficiency, use a collar-friction term for accuracy.

glossary.def: A framework of straight members pin-jointed at their ends, loaded only at the joints, used for roofs, bridges and towers.
A pin connection where two or more members of a truss meet and where external loads are applied.
An axial member force that pulls the joint, so the member is stretched.
An axial member force that pushes the joint, so the member is shortened.
The force or moment a support exerts on a body to keep it in place, found from the equilibrium equations.
A sketch of one body alone with every external force drawn on it, the starting point of every statics solution.
A connection that can transmit force in any direction but cannot transmit a moment.
A support that gives only a reaction normal to the surface it rests on.
Friction that acts while the body is still at rest, adjustable up to the limiting value μN.
Friction acting while surfaces slide; usually slightly smaller than the limiting static value.
The state just before sliding starts, where friction has reached its limit μN.
The dimensionless ratio of limiting friction to normal reaction between two given surfaces.
The cone of semi-vertical angle φ swept by the resultant reaction as it tilts around the normal.
The inclination of a rough plane at which a block just begins to slide, numerically equal to the angle of friction.
A triangular block used to lift, split or clamp, working by friction on two inclined faces.
A helical ridge on a cylinder that converts rotation into axial motion, as in a screw jack.
The axial distance between consecutive threads of a screw.
The axial distance a screw advances in one complete turn, equal to pitch for a single-start thread.
The property of a screw or wedge by which friction alone holds the load and prevents it from running back.
Useful work output divided by work input; for a screw jack, tan α / tan(α + φ).
A pair of pulleys joined by a belt, transmitting power through the difference of the two belt tensions.
The angle, in radians, over which the belt touches the pulley; it sets the tension ratio together with μ.
